claim: AWS security best practice: unless you explicitly need anyone on the internet to read or write the bucket, make sure the bucket is not public.
question: What is the first S3 security best practice about public access?

values.display: make sure that your S3 bucket is not public

qualifiers.condition: unless you explicitly require public read or write access

evidence.quote: Unless you explicitly require anyone on the internet to be able to read or write to your S3 bucket, make sure that your S3 bucket is not public.

claim: S3 Block Public Access gives centralized controls that limit public access to S3 resources, and these controls are enforced regardless of how the resources were created; it can also be enforced organization-wide through AWS Organizations.
question: What makes S3 Block Public Access stronger than reviewing each bucket policy?

values.display: enforced regardless of how the resources are created
organization-level enforcement through AWS Organizations

qualifiers.scope: per account, per bucket, or per organization

evidence.quote: With S3 Block Public Access, you can easily set up centralized controls to limit public access to your Amazon S3 resources. These centralized controls are enforced regardless of how the resources are created. For organizations managing multiple AWS accounts, you can now use organization-level enforcement through AWS Organizations to centrally manage S3 Block Public Access settings across your entire organization with a single policy configuration.

claim: A bucket policy that allows a wildcard identity, "Principal": "*", effectively means anyone; a wildcard action "*" allows any action in the bucket. Both are signs of a public or over-permissive bucket.
question: What does Principal "*" mean in a bucket policy?

values.display: which effectively means "anyone"
which effectively allows the user to perform any action in the Amazon S3 bucket

evidence.quote: Identify Amazon S3 bucket policies that allow a wildcard identity such as `"Principal": "*"` (which effectively means "anyone"). Also look for policies that allow a wildcard action `"*"` (which effectively allows the user to perform any action in the Amazon S3 bucket).

claim: AWS recommends not storing AWS credentials in an application or EC2 instance; use an IAM role so the application gets temporary credentials for S3 access.
question: How should an application on EC2 or Lambda get its S3 permissions?

values.display: use an IAM role to manage temporary credentials
not storing AWS credentials directly in the application or Amazon EC2 instance

qualifiers.scope: applications on EC2 and other AWS services

evidence.quote: We recommend not storing AWS credentials directly in the application or Amazon EC2 instance. These are long-term credentials that are not automatically rotated and could have a significant business impact if they are compromised.
Instead, use an IAM role to manage temporary credentials for applications or services that need to access Amazon S3.

claim: Every S3 bucket has encryption configured, with SSE-S3 as the default; to use another type (SSE-KMS, DSSE-KMS, SSE-C) you either name it in the PUT request or set the bucket's default encryption configuration.
question: How do you move a bucket, or a single object, from SSE-S3 to SSE-KMS?

values.display: Server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3) is the default encryption configuration for every bucket
specify the type of server-side encryption to use in your S3 PUT requests, or you can set the default encryption configuration in the destination bucket

qualifiers.scope: per bucket (default) and per object (PUT request)

evidence.quote: Server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3) is the default encryption configuration for every bucket in Amazon S3. To use a different type of encryption, you can either specify the type of server-side encryption to use in your S3 `PUT` requests, or you can set the default encryption configuration in the destination bucket.

claim: SSE-C needs the encryption key in every read or write request, which makes sharing access with other users, roles or AWS services impractical; AWS managed services cannot natively decrypt SSE-C objects. SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS give equal protection with more flexibility.
question: Why is SSE-C the wrong answer when other AWS services must read the objects?

values.display: provide the encryption key with every request
cannot be natively decrypted by AWS managed services

evidence.quote: SSE-C requires you to provide the encryption key with every request to read or write encrypted objects. This makes it impractical to share access with other users, roles, or AWS services that operate on your data. Objects encrypted with SSE-C cannot be natively decrypted by AWS managed services. For most workloads, server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3) or AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS) provides equivalent protection with greater flexibility.

claim: With client-side encryption you encrypt the data before upload and you manage the encryption process, the keys and the tools; the key is held apart from the data store.
question: What changes for you when you choose client-side encryption instead of server-side encryption?

values.display: you manage the encryption process, the encryption keys, and related tools

evidence.quote: Encrypt data client-side and upload the encrypted data to Amazon S3. In this case, you manage the encryption process, the encryption keys, and related tools.

claim: HTTPS (TLS) protects S3 traffic from eavesdropping and person-in-the-middle manipulation; AWS recommends allowing only encrypted HTTPS connections through a bucket policy condition.
question: How do you enforce encryption in transit for an S3 bucket?

values.display: allowing only encrypted connections over HTTPS (TLS)
eavesdropping on or manipulating network traffic

qualifiers.condition: bucket policy with the aws:SecureTransport condition

evidence.quote: You can use HTTPS (TLS) to help prevent potential attackers from eavesdropping on or manipulating network traffic by using person-in-the-middle or similar attacks. We recommend allowing only encrypted connections over HTTPS (TLS) by using the [aws:SecureTransport](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_elements_condition_operators.html#Conditions_Boolean) condition in your Amazon S3 bucket policies.

claim: S3 Object Lock stores objects in a write-once-read-many (WORM) model and helps prevent accidental or inappropriate deletion, for example of CloudTrail logs.
question: Which S3 feature gives WORM storage?

values.display: "Write Once Read Many" (WORM) model
help prevent accidental or inappropriate deletion of data

qualifiers.scope: per bucket with Object Lock enabled

evidence.quote: With S3 Object Lock, you can store objects by using a "Write Once Read Many" (WORM) model. S3 Object Lock can help prevent accidental or inappropriate deletion of data. For example, you can use S3 Object Lock to help protect your AWS CloudTrail logs.

claim: S3 already stores data across several geographically separate Availability Zones; when compliance requires copies at a greater distance, Cross-Region Replication copies objects automatically and asynchronously to a bucket in a distant Region.
question: When does an exam scenario need Cross-Region Replication rather than S3's built-in multi-AZ redundancy?

values.display: compliance requirements might dictate that you store data at even greater distances
automatic, asynchronous copying of objects across buckets in different AWS Regions

evidence.quote: Although Amazon S3 stores your data across multiple geographically diverse Availability Zones by default, compliance requirements might dictate that you store data at even greater distances. With S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR), you can replicate data between distant AWS Regions to help satisfy these requirements. CRR enables automatic, asynchronous copying of objects across buckets in different AWS Regions.

claim: Cross-Region Replication requires versioning to be enabled on both the source bucket and the destination bucket.
question: What must be turned on before you can configure Cross-Region Replication?

values.display: both the source and destination S3 buckets to have versioning enabled

qualifiers.scope: source and destination buckets of a replication rule

evidence.quote: CRR requires both the source and destination S3 buckets to have versioning enabled.

claim: A VPC endpoint for S3 is a logical entity inside a VPC that connects only to S3, so traffic does not cross the open internet; bucket policies can restrict access to a given VPC or endpoint, and a VPC without an internet gateway limits data exfiltration.
question: How do you give private instances S3 access without crossing the internet, and lock the bucket to that path?

values.display: help prevent traffic from traversing the open internet
control which VPCs or VPC endpoints have access to your S3 buckets by using S3 bucket policies
help prevent data exfiltration by using a VPC that does not have an internet gateway

qualifiers.scope: per VPC endpoint and per bucket policy

evidence.quote: A virtual private cloud (VPC) endpoint for Amazon S3 is a logical entity within a VPC that allows connectivity only to Amazon S3. VPC endpoints can help prevent traffic from traversing the open internet.
You can control which VPCs or VPC endpoints have access to your S3 buckets by using S3 bucket policies.
You can help prevent data exfiltration by using a VPC that does not have an internet gateway.

claim: Server access logging records every request made to a bucket in detail, for security and access audits and for understanding the S3 bill.
question: Which S3 feature gives detailed request-level records for an audit?

values.display: detailed records of the requests that are made to a bucket

evidence.quote: Server access logging provides detailed records of the requests that are made to a bucket. Server access logs can assist you in security and access audits, help you learn about your customer base, and understand your Amazon S3 bill.

claim: AWS recommends granting only the permissions required to perform a task (least privilege) on S3 resources, to reduce the impact of errors or malicious intent.
question: What does least privilege mean for S3 permissions?

values.display: grant only the permissions that are required to perform a task

qualifiers.scope: IAM and bucket policies for S3

evidence.quote: Therefore, we recommend that you grant only the permissions that are required to perform a task. Implementing least privilege access is fundamental in reducing security risk and the impact that could result from errors or malicious intent.

claim: The Well-Architected security pillar notes that Amazon S3 now encrypts all new objects by default, with no impact on performance.
question: Does the Well-Architected Framework still ask you to turn on S3 encryption by hand?

values.display: now encrypt all new objects by default
no impact on performance

evidence.quote: Additionally, services such as Amazon Simple Storage Service ([Amazon S3](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/amazon-s3-encrypts-new-objects-by-default/)) now encrypt all new objects by default. This implementation provides enhanced security with no impact on performance.

claim: Well-Architected guidance: AWS-managed and service-controlled KMS keys are used on your behalf by AWS; for sensitive data that needs fine-grained control of the key, use customer managed keys, which you fully control including rotation and key policies.
question: When does the exam expect a customer managed KMS key instead of the AWS managed key?

values.display: sensitive data that requires fine-grained access to the underlying encryption key
full control over CMKs, including rotation and access management through the use of key policies

qualifiers.scope: AWS KMS keys used for S3 server-side encryption

evidence.quote: Default and service-controlled AWS KMS keys are managed and used on your behalf by AWS. For sensitive data that requires fine-grained access to the underlying encryption key, consider customer managed keys (CMKs). You have full control over CMKs, including rotation and access management through the use of key policies.

claim: Well-Architected guidance: map encryption keys to data classifications, for example one KMS key for production data and another for development or test data, instead of one key for everything.
question: How many KMS keys should a workload with several data classes use?

values.display: Map encryption keys to data classifications
one AWS KMS key for encrypting production data and a different key for encrypting development or test data

evidence.quote: Map encryption keys to data classifications within your workloads. This approach helps protect against overly permissive access when using either a single, or very small number of encryption keys for your data (see [SEC07-BP01 Understand your data classification scheme](sec_data_classification_identify_data.md)).
For example, create one AWS KMS key for encrypting production data and a different key for encrypting development or test data.

claim: Well-Architected guidance: S3 Object Lock gives mandatory access control that prevents objects from being deleted or overwritten, even by the root user, until the lock expires; Amazon Glacier Vault Lock does the same for Glacier vault archives.
question: Which control stops even the root user from deleting an S3 object before a retention date?

values.display: prevents them from being deleted or overwritten, even by the root user, until the lock expires
Amazon Glacier Vault Lock

evidence.quote: [Amazon S3 Object Lock](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock.html) provides mandatory access control for objects, which prevents them from being deleted or overwritten, even by the root user, until the lock expires. Additionally, [Amazon Glacier Vault Lock](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazonglacier/latest/dev/vault-lock.html) offers a similar feature for archives stored in Amazon Glacier.

claim: Well-Architected guidance: review bucket policies regularly, avoid publicly readable or writable buckets unless absolutely necessary, detect public buckets with AWS Config, and serve content from S3 through Amazon CloudFront.
question: What does the Well-Architected Framework recommend instead of a public bucket for serving content?

values.display: Avoid using publicly readable or writeable buckets unless absolutely necessary
Amazon CloudFront to serve content from Amazon S3

evidence.quote: Regularly review the level of access granted in Amazon S3 bucket policies. Avoid using publicly readable or writeable buckets unless absolutely necessary. Consider using [AWS Config](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/config/latest/developerguide/managed-rules-by-aws-config.html) to detect publicly available buckets and Amazon CloudFront to serve content from Amazon S3.

claim: IAM Access Analyzer can analyze S3 buckets and raise a finding when a bucket policy grants access to an external entity.
question: Which service finds S3 buckets that are shared outside your account?

values.display: generate findings when an S3 policy grants access to an external entity

evidence.quote: You can configure [AWS IAM Access Analyzer](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/what-is-access-analyzer.html) to analyze Amazon S3 buckets and generate findings when an S3 policy grants access to an external entity.

claim: Well-Architected guidance: separate data of different classification levels into distinct AWS accounts managed with AWS Organizations, to isolate it and lower the risk of exposure.
question: How does the Well-Architected Framework isolate data of different sensitivity?

values.display: distinct AWS accounts for each level

evidence.quote: You can separate data based on different classification levels by using distinct AWS accounts for each level, and manage these accounts using [AWS Organizations](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_introduction.html). This isolation can help prevent unauthorized access and minimizes the risk of data exposure.

claim: S3 Inventory audits and reports the replication and encryption status of objects, for business, compliance and regulatory needs.
question: Which S3 feature reports which objects are encrypted or replicated?

values.display: audit and report on the replication and encryption status of your objects

evidence.quote: Use S3 Inventory to audit and report on the replication and encryption status of your objects for business, compliance, and regulatory needs.

claim: AWS Backup can back up an S3 bucket only after S3 Versioning is activated on that bucket.
question: What must be enabled on a bucket before AWS Backup can protect it?

values.display: activate S3 Versioning on your bucket before AWS Backup can back it up

evidence.quote: You must activate [S3 Versioning](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/Versioning.html) on your bucket before AWS Backup can back it up.

claim: AWS Backup for S3 offers continuous backups for point-in-time restore and periodic backups for long-term retention; alongside it, S3 Versioning and S3 Replication support self-recovery from accidental deletions.
question: When do you pick AWS Backup for S3 over versioning or replication?

values.display: Continuous backups are useful for point-in-time restore
periodic backups are useful to meet your long-term data-retention needs

evidence.quote: Create continuous backups and periodic backups. Continuous backups are useful for point-in-time restore, and periodic backups are useful to meet your long-term data-retention needs.
Along with AWS Backup, you can use S3 Versioning and S3 Replication to help recover from accidental deletions and perform your own self-recovery operations.

claim: For a versioned bucket that AWS Backup protects, set a lifecycle expiration rule; otherwise storage cost can grow because every version is retained.
question: Why can a versioned, backed-up bucket get expensive, and what rule prevents it?

values.display: your Amazon S3 storage costs might increase because AWS Backup retains all versions
set a lifecycle expiration rule for versioning-enabled buckets

qualifiers.scope: versioning-enabled buckets backed up by AWS Backup

evidence.quote: We recommend that you [ set a lifecycle expiration rule for versioning-enabled buckets](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/lifecycle-configuration-examples.html#lifecycle-config-conceptual-ex6) that are being backed up. If you do not set a lifecycle expiration period, your Amazon S3 storage costs might increase because AWS Backup retains all versions of your Amazon S3 data.
